texts.preamble: Sh. Upender Kumar Mehto vs Sh. Bal Mukand on 24 October, 2019 In The Court Of Sh. Yashwant Kumar District & Sessions Judge/Fsat: Patiala House Courts New Delhi In the matter of : Fsat No. 06/17 Cnr No. : Dlnd010020962017 1. Sh. Upender Kumar Mehto S/o Sh. Ram Dev Mehto M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd. R4 Inderpuri Commercial Area New Delhi110 012. 2. M/s Buttercup Confectionary Ltd. R4 Inderpuri Commercial Area New Delhi110 012. Through Authorised Representative ... Appellants Versus Sh. Bal Mukand Food Safety Officer Department of Food Safety Govt. of Delhi 8th Floor, Mayur Bhawan Connaught Place, New Delhi110001. ..... Respondent Appeal Against The Order Dated 24.05.2016 Of Ld. Adjudicating Officer, District (New Delhi) Judgment
texts.facts: 2. Facts in brief as per the appeal are that on 26.10.2013, Food Safety Officer ("FSO" in short), had taken the sample of "Filled Chocolate & Composite Chocolate", from the premises of M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd., Inderpuri, New Delhi, for analysis. The Food Analyst vide his report dated 11.11.2013 reported that the sample contains extraneous matter viz. added vegetable fats in contravention of Regulation no.2.7.4 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011 read with Section 3(1)(i) of FSS Act, 2006. The Food Safety Officer filed a application under Rule 3.1.1(3) FSS Rules, 2011 before the Ld. ADM alleging violation of Section 26(2)(ii), Section 27(1) read with Section 3(1)(i) of Sh. Upender Kumar Mehto vs Sh. Bal Mukand on 24 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65785799/ 1 FSS Act and Regulation no.2.7.4 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, punishable under Section 54 of FSS Act. Notice of the same was issued to the appellants and hearing was given. 3. The appellants have challenged the impugned order inter alia on the grounds that Ld. ADM has wrongly interpreted the law on the subject and did not appreciate the prescribed standards applicable to the sampled commodity as per Regulation No. 2.7.4 of FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations, 2011. The Ld. ADM did not appreciate the fact and law that as per standards of Filled Chocolates, only 25% Chocolate out of other six types of chocolates should be used in outer layer and rest of the filled chocolate can have confectionery product in centre in which vanaspati is not prohibited. In the filled chocolate, vanaspati was used as an ingredient only in the centre of the product which is not prohibited as per law applicable. However, vanaspati is not permitted only in the outer layer of filled chocolate where 25% chocolate is required to be used in filled chocolate as per given standards. Ld. ADM failed to appreciate that the Food Analyst has adopted the wrong procedure in analyzing the sampled commodity as it has come in the crossexamination that the testing of sample of filled chocolate was done by mixing the whole contents i.e. outer and inner layer both and not by testing the outer layer and central layer separately, resulting in forming of wrong opinion by the Food Analyst. 4. The Ld. Chief PP for the respondent/State has not filed reply to the main appeal. However, he has opposed the same. 8. Perusal of the record reveals that this appeal has been filed by the appellants against the said impugned order dated 24.05.2016 passed by the Ld. , thereby he imposed a Sh. Upender Kumar Mehto vs Sh. Bal Mukand on 24 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65785799/ 2 consolidated penalty of Rs. 1 Lakh for selling the product containing extraneous matter attracting the penalty as per Section 54 of FSS Act, 2006. The appellants in their appeal stated that they are engaged in manufacturing chocolates and other confectionery products. The said Food Safety Officer took the sample of food article as discussed above from the premises of appellant no.2 for analysis by Food Analyst, on 26.10.2013 and he reported the sample as containing extraneous matter added vegetable fat convening the Regulation No. 2.7.4 of FSS Regulations, 2011 read with Section 3(1)(i) of FSS Act, 2006.
texts.arguments: 6. Ld. Counsel for the appellants argued that the Adjudicating Officer did not appreciate the prescribed standards applicable to the sampled commodity as per Regulation No. 2.7.4 of "FSS (FPS & FA) Regulations". In the filled chocolate Vanaspati was used as an ingredient only in the centre of the product which is not prohibited as per law applicable. Wrong procedure was adopted in analyzing the sampled commodity. Testing the sample was done by mixing the whole contents i.e. outer and inner layer, which resulted in wrong opinion by Food Analyst. No loss was caused or likely to cause to any person due to such erroneous alleged contravention. The appellant company is old reputed manufacturer of quality confectionery and chocolates. In support of his arguments, Ld. Counsel for the appellants has relied upon the reported judgments in cases of Pawan Kumar Agarwal Vs. The State of Jharkhand & another 2012(1) FAC 449 and Harish Chand versus State in Criminal Revision No. 100 of 1970 decided by Hon'ble Delhi High Court on 14.05.1970. 7. Ld. Chief PP for the State argued that the FSS Act has been amended in the year 2017. As per the said amendment, the vegetable oil can now be added in the Chocolates. The case of the appellants may be considered by this court as per the provisions of FSS Act/Regulations and also of the judgments passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and Delhi High Court in this regard. The appellants have stated that the Ld. Adjudicating Officer did not appreciate the prescribed standards applicable to the sampled commodity as per the said provisions and wrongly interpreted the law on the abovesaid article. As per the standards of filled chocolates, only 25% chocolate out of 6 types of chocolate should be used in outer layer and rest of the filled chocolate can have confectionery product in the centre in which Vanaspati is not prohibited. Therefore, in the filled chocolate, Vanaspati was used as an ingredient only in the centre of the product which is not prohibited as per law applicable. However, Vanaspati is not permitted only in outer layer of filled chocolate where 25% chocolate is required to be used in filled chocolate as per given standards. 9. In this context, the case of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan 2016 (1) FAC 561 is referred, thereby the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that "since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court." The relevant para quoted in the said judgment of Nemi Chand (Supra), is reproduced as under : "3. Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below. He has in this behalf, argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable. He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in 'T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe and Another' [1982 (2) FAC 362] [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court. In the said judgment, the Court held as under: "22. It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1). The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. But insofar as the Central Amendment Sh. Upender Kumar Mehto vs Sh. Bal Mukand on 24 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65785799/ 3 Act reduces the punishment for an offence punishable under Section 16(1) (a) of the Act, there is no reason why the accused should not have the benefit of such reduced punishment. The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law. The principle is based both on sound reason and common sense. This finds support in the following passage from Crales on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 38889: A retrospective statute is different from an ex post facto statute. "Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law. Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon. They are certainly retrospective, and literally both concerning and after the facts committed. But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law, but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence for the purpose of conviction.... There is a great and apparent difference between making an unlawful act lawful and the making an innocent action criminal and punishing it as a crime." 10.
